title: Faith
hookLine: faith is the substance of things hoped for
tomorrow: what's the difference between hope and wishful thinking?

cards: Nobody tests a chair before sitting in it. You get into a car with a driver you met thirty seconds ago. You eat food a stranger cooked.

Whole days run on trust you never proved. The Letter to the Hebrews gives faith a definition, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now faith is the substance of things to be hoped for, the evidence of things that appear not."
Evidence of what you can't see. So where does that come from? Catholics have two honest answers, and they pull in different directions.

teach.b: The first answer: faith is a gift. You can't argue yourself into it or work it up by trying harder. The Catechism calls it a gift of God, a virtue he pours in.
The best case for this view is real: it explains why two people can hear the same reasons and only one believes, and it takes the pressure off. Nobody earns it.
The second answer: faith is a choice. The same Catechism says believing is a truly human act, free, never forced, and not against reason.
The best case here is real too: it treats the believer as a person who says yes, not a container that got filled.
Thomas Aquinas puts the mind and the will together: the mind agrees, because the will, moved by grace, chooses to. So which is it?

teach.h: I DO BELIEVE, HELP MY UNBELIEF.
teach.b: Mark's Gospel has a father with a sick son who answers in one breath, in the Douay-Rheims: "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief." I do believe: that's his choice. Help my unbelief: that's asking for the gift.

teach.h: THE CREED STARTS WITH A PERSON.
teach.b: Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Creed Catholics say at Mass doesn't begin with God exists.
It begins with I believe, a person speaking.

how: Catholics profess their faith in the Creed at Sunday Mass, and some pray a short traditional Act of Faith in the morning or before confession.

o: a feeling of calm that comes during prayer
trust in what you can't see, given and chosen
being sure of something because it's been proven

games.q: two answers, one father — tap the pairs.

s: Catholic teaching says faith is against reason
the Catechism says believing is a free human act and not against reason.
the Creed at Mass opens with the words I believe
it begins with a person speaking, not a bare statement.
having doubts means you have no faith
the father in Mark says both in one breath: I do believe; help my unbelief.

games.q: your friend says, "if faith is a gift, then it's not my fault i don't have it." what's the strongest answer from inside the Catholic view?
o: you're right, so there's nothing for you to do.
it's a gift and a free yes: you can still ask, like the father.
faith is just a choice; try harder and it will come.
games.why: the Catechism holds both: faith is God's gift and a free human act. the father in Mark chooses and asks at once: I do believe; help my unbelief.

practice: Say the two words out loud, quietly: I believe. Then add one thing you can honestly put after them, anything at all.
If you pray, the Creed's own opening is yours: I believe in God; and if part of you doubts, the father's words fit right beside it: help my unbelief.

wordCard.voice: Faith. The evidence of things unseen, which Catholics call both God's gift and a free yes.

orig.note: Greek: faith, trust. the word in Hebrews 11:1.

carryVoice: Carry this: I believe, two small words with a whole person standing behind them. Until tomorrow.
